speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the people of northern Ontario are angry because the Government has caved in to the Americans and agreed to an arrangement for making permanent a 15 per cent cost imposition on our softwood lumber. Whether that 15 per cent is a tariff, an export tax, or an increase in stumpage fees, the result will be equally devastating for northern Ontario. Saw mills are and will be closed. Thousands of jobs will be lost. The industry in Ontario cannot afford the burden of an additional 15 per cent cost. Even if the $600 million or $700 million referred to by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) remains in Canada, it cannot be poured back into the industry without risking a further 15 per cent from the Americans.
We in Canada have the sovereign right to place a value on our natural resources. For the Americans to try to dictate the worth of our resources is a violation of our sovereignty. We should have stood our ground and fought. Instead, we yielded to American pressure. Today we gave in on lumber. Tomorrow it may be pulp or paper. We in northern Ontario feel betrayed and we will not forget this act of unfairness and injustice.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the federal Government has made genuine progress in making the environment safer for people who have allergies. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) has banned the use of sulphites so that people will no longer risk having an allergic reaction to food which they eat in restaurants or buy at a store.
However, more needs to be done. Every time we take a drug we risk having an allergic reaction because the ingredients of drugs are not listed on the label and we do not really know what is contained therein. One Canadian died this year when she unknowingly took a drug which contained a preservative to which she was allergic. Another Canadian has been near death on several occasions because he did not know that the drug he was taking contained an ingredient to which he was allergic.
These situations could have been avoided if the ingredients of the drugs were listed on the labels. Ingredients of drugs should not be kept a secret. Canada has one of the best ingredient lists on foods in the world. I urge the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) to apply those same standards to medication.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, an Air Canada employee in Winnipeg was fired on October 14 on the basis of a drug test. I understand that the worker was not informed that he would have to undergo the drug test performed by an Air Canada physician as part of a mandatory medical examination, and that a number of other applicants for the same job were not informed that they would have to undergo similar testing.
This man was hired on August 15 and worked for almost two months before being fired on the basis of a finding of cannabis in his test taken prior to being hired. An Air Canada official has stated that the worker's job performance was not even taken into consideration. The employee states that he discontinued the use of marijuana when he was hired at Air Canada, and went back to the same clinic which Air Canada, uses for another drug screen. The test revealed no trace of the drug.
I believe that this is an example of indiscriminate drug testing by Air Canada. Air Canada is particularly despicable in its use of the tests for failing to inform applicants that they will be screened for drugs and, in this particular instance, for firing someone on the basis of a two-month old drug test without even giving any consideration to the person's performance record on the job. The Minister responsible for Air Canada should end this questionable practice immediately.

Mr. Speaker, Doctor Ken Hare, a climatology expert, says that "the greenhouse effect" is a reality. He predicts that temperatures in the Arctic will rise by as much as eight degrees by the year 2040 and that the planet will be affected, with particular impact on Canada.
As a nation we will have to make major adjustments to cope with the rise in temperature. I urge the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) to develop an action plan on the greenhouse effect. This is a complex and inter-generational issue. We must ensure that as a nation we are equipped to deal with the changes that the rise in global temperature will bring about.
We also ought to help plan a global response and set up the international structures needed to tackle a global issue of such magnitude. Let us hope that the World Commission on Environment and Development will design the international structures necessary to slow down, if not check, the greenhouse effect, and that the United Nations will act on their recommendations expeditiously.

Mr. Speaker, once again, our Conservative Government is keeping its promises to Canadian taxpayers by maintaining and promoting the universality of social programs, including family allowances. Our Government has made it possible for 756,000 families with incomes of less than $15,000 in 1985 to receive advance payments for 1986 of $300 per child, and this will apply to about 1,300,000 children in Canada.
This year, the maximum child tax credit payable in the spring of 1987 will be $454, an increase of $70, and in 1988 the maximum will be $524. This means that from now on families will no longer have to resort to using the services of tax discounters who in some cases were taking advantage of the precarious financial situation of low-income Canadian families. Mr. Speaker, this is one more example of the sense of equity and justice that guides this Government.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Chair is advised that the last Member to speak in debate was from the Liberal Party. Therefore, I think it would be appropriate, since there is no government Member standing to be recognized, to recognize the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson).

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today to take part in this very important debate on a matter which affects literally hundreds of thousands of Canadians directly and virtually all Canadians indirectly.
I and my colleagues in the New Democratic Party have strongly opposed Bill C-22 which is being proposed by the Conservative Government since it first attempted to introduce it this spring. And on a previous occasion when the former Liberal Government made moves to weaken the protection which was accorded to the producers of generic drugs we put that Government on notice that we would not stand idly by
Patent Act
and allow these protections, which were initially implemented in 1969, to be in any way weakened to the detriment of those who are the most vulnerable in our society.
All Members of Parliament have received many representations on this legislation. I want to give a couple of illustrations of the kinds of responses I have received from my constituents as the Member of Parliament for Burnaby. I quote from a letter received from a gentleman and his wife who live on Gatenby Avenue in Burnaby;
Both my wife and I suffer from chronic ailments requiring constant medication. The cost of these drugs is already high, especially to one like myself who is on pension. Any major increase would be an additional strain on our finances.
I urge you and your Party to take energetic measures to block the passage of any legislation that would increase the price of drugs.
I have heard the same thing from many senior citizens in my constituency who live in the Winch Towers, the Vista Towers Senior Citizen's Complex, Doug Drummond Manor, the Hall Towers Senior Citizen's Complex, and from many others I could name if time permitted. However, in the interests of moving along in the debate I will not name all of them. Suffice it to say that these people share a sense of anger and a sense of deep concern that drugs which are already too expensive may increase in price.
We have to ask ourselves why this Conservative Government chooses to move forward at this time with a Bill which would increase the price of drugs to Canadians. What we are told is that if in fact the compulsory licencing provisions which were introduced in 1969 are eliminated it would somehow encourage more research in Canada and create more jobs. That does not make any sense. Before 1969 there was no compulsory licencing, yet Canada had some of the highest drug prices in the world, and before there was compulsory licencing there was a very low level of research on new drugs. Therefore, this myth that somehow there will be a significant increase in the level of research and development is merely a carrot being dangled by the Government and the multinational drug industry in an attempt to obtain protection under the Patent Act.
We in this Party do not buy that kind of corporate bribery. We certainly reject the suggestion that the consumers of Canada, the disabled, the poor, the seniors and those who are least able to afford drugs should be required to bear the burden of this Conservative Government's ideological fixation with paying off American multinational drug companies.
The Minister for Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) has said there will be no significant increase in the price of drugs; in fact, he said there will be no increase in the price of drugs. Why is it that the same Minister has refused to make public the cost impact studies of this particular Bill? What does he have to hide? If in fact the studies, paid for after all by the taxpayers of Canada, disclose that there will be no increase in the price of drugs, we all know he would be the first

November 25, 1986
Patent Act
person to table those studies here in the Elouse of Commons. We know the truth, Mr. Speaker, and the truth is that the cost impact studies commissioned by the Government show that the Minister is not levelling with the people of Canada when he says there will be no increase in the price of drugs.
What does that mean in real terms? Let us take a couple of examples of the drugs with which we are dealing. One of the more common drugs used in Canada is the drug Tagamet. It is very widely used by people who have ulcers. One hundred tablets of the brand name drug Tagamet costs approximately $40 in Vancouver. The generic equivalent of Tagamet costs approximately $15.1 know Hon. Members of the House would not want to move forward legislation which could in effect significantly increase the level of drug prices such as Tagamet.
One of the newer antibiotics brand name drugs, Amoxicillin, costs approximately $18. The generic equivalent costs about $9, about half that price. One of the most widely prescribed drugs in Canada is Valium. In Winnipeg, for example, the retail price for 100 tablets of the brand name drug Valium is approximately $15. The retail price for the generic equivalent is just a little over $5.
I think my constituents in Burnaby and, indeed, the people of Canada, have a right to know why it is the Government is caving in to the pressure of the American multinational drug companies. Is it not a fact that the real hidden agenda here is that the Tory Government is trying to grease the skids for its free trade negotiations with the Americans? We know, for example, that Clayton Yeutter, the chief American negotiator on free trade, has put strong pressure on the Canadian Government to move forward, to increase the price of drugs. He said that drug prices will rise. For example, he said:
Any improvements in this area are clearly in the best interest of Canada as a nation. Now in some cases maybe this will raise the price at the retail level of some of these products, but if we're going to have low retail prices based upon piracy it seems to me that's not a sound way to run a country.
At least Clayton Yeutter has the honesty to level with Canadians that the prices of drugs in Canada will rise.
Professor Eastman, who headed up a commission in this area, was very clear that the long-term prices of prescription drugs in Canada will increase as a result of this Bill. The Minister himself has effectively conceded to the consumers of Canada that drug prices will increase. On the one hand he said, no, there will be no increase in the price of drugs to Canadians. On the other hand, when dealing with the provinces, he said: "What I will do is put aside $25 million a year for four years". The reason for that is to cover the increase in the price of drugs to their pharmacare plans. So the Minister is saying one thing to provincial Ministers of Health, and at the same time the Minister is speaking out of the other side of his mouth to consumers telling them there will be no increase in price. If there is no increase in the price of drugs, why on earth does the Minister have to guarantee to provincial pharmacare plans that he will give them more money? The only possible reason for giving them more money would be to increase the profits of the multinational drug companies. We already know
that this has been one of the most profitable sectors in Canadian society.
I would like to take a moment to address the question of a health care system and, more particularly, an industry which is geared solely to the pursuit of profit. I want to suggest that as democratic socialists, and as Members of the New Democratic Party, we believe there are certain sectors of the economy which should not be driven solely by the pursuit of profit and greed but which should be based upon the effective serving of human needs. I can think of no more appropriate sector for that particular philosophical approach than the health care sector. As long ago as 1961 my Party in its founding documents spoke clearly and with great eloquence about the importance of a health care system in which all of the health care needs of Canadians would be served and in which no Canadian would be deprived of affordable health care because he or she could not afford drugs, dental care or decent medical care.
In 1975, at the federal convention of my Party, we proposed and adopted the following resolution. It was arrived at after discussing the deterioration of health care and the fact that the fundamental principles which were the cornerstone of our medicare system were being eroded; fundamental principles which people such as Tommy Douglas, Woodrow Lloyd, Allen Blakeney and other New Democrats and CCFers fought long and hard to establish.
In our resolution we stated that we should be extending federal-provincial cost-sharing of services to include all extended health care services currently provided in some provinces but not others. There are still provinces today which do not offer their citizens pharmacare plans. What this means is that if one is a poor person living in one of those provinces and if one happens to be sick, disabled or dependent upon a particular drug, then he or she will suffer.
I am proud of the fact that it was a NDP Government in my own Province of British Columbia which introduced a pharmacare system in 1973. I hope that Governments all across the country will recognize the obligation to their citizens, and that no one should be forced into poverty because he or she happens to be sick and needs drugs.
One of the essential elements of the health care resolution that was adopted by the New Democratic Party in 1975 was that a NDP Government would assist the provinces to reform the health care system by setting up a Crown corporation to manufacture and bulk purchase low-cost generic equivalents of the 80 most common drugs prescribed. There are some who say that that is a radical proposal. They ask: "What about the free enterprise system? What about competition in the marketplace?" In that respect let us look at the underlying premises of the Patent Act.
By adopting the legislation which is proposed by the Tory Government what we are saying is that the only way that we

can encourage the development of new drugs in our society is, effectively to bribe the corporate sector by giving it the exclusive rights to drugs for a period of 10 years. What type of a distorted approach is that to health care? In this country, and, indeed, globally-and I can talk at some length about the abuses of multinational drug corporations in Third World countries where there is the dumping of substandard drugs and, indeed, in some cases, hazardous drugs-it is fundamentally wrong for us to adopt an approach in which effectively we say to the multinational drug companies that we have sicknesses and diseases in our society which we want treated. Our citizens have pains and disabilities which require drug treatment. We want you as a corporate community to assist us in responding to this pain, this suffering and this sickness. The only way that we as a Government are prepared to move forward on this issue is to give you exclusive rights for 10 years to the patent. I say that that is nonsense. We should be adopting a fundamentally different approach.
As a society we should be saying that if drugs are developed to deal with illness, pain and suffering, then we should not have to bribe the corporate sector with guarantees of exclusivity for 10 years to develop those drugs. No. We should be saying to the scientists in our society that we believe the best minds in the country, the best men and women scientists in the country, should be working collectively to develop responses to illness and pain. We should not have to bribe multinational corporations to conduct research in secret laboratories or have scientists working in splendid isolation from one another on cures for the same disease. That approach to health care is fundamentally immoral.
I suggest we have to look at the underpinnings of this legislation. We must recognize that when it comes to the provision of health care services and to the provision of quality drugs this approach is profoundly wrong. I suggest that the Government is caving in to the demands of American multinational corporations without any guarantees whatsoever that there will be any significant increase in research in Canada.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), who has led the fight on behalf of our caucus with respect to this Bill, said that there was no significant research done prior to 1969 and the advent of compulsory licensing. The companies about which we are talking are major multinationals, European and American companies which have labs in their home countries. They are not going to do research in any significant degree in Canada. They will do it in labs in their own jurisdictions. It is nonsense to suggest otherwise.
Earlier I mentioned the letter I received from the pensioners in my constituency of Burnaby who suffer from chronic ailments requiring constant medication. I have received letters as well from those who are disabled and who rely on drugs to help make their lives bearable, to help ease the pain. The Tory Government is saying to those who are most vulnerable, to those who depend on drugs to make their lives a little more bearable, that we will increase the price of those drugs. Why? Because we have been promised by American multinationals

that they will create jobs in Canada. I do not buy that promise.
1 do not buy it because there is no evidence to back it up. I do not buy the promise of the Minister that prices will not increase when the evidence is clear that they will. The Minister has not even had the courage to table in the House the studies which were done by his Department at the expense of the taxpayers of Canada which deal with the impact in terms of costs.
In conclusion, I wish to make it clear that I and my colleagues in this Party are proud of the tradition of the New Democratic Party, both provincially and federally, in terms of standing up for an effective health care system in Canada. We will do everything-and I underline the word "everything"-in our power to prevent the Conservative Government from caving in to the pressure of multinational corporations in a way that will result in increases in the price of generic drugs, indeed, in the price of all drugs, an increase which will hit those who are most vulnerable, the sick, the disabled and seniors.

We are speaking up on behalf of those who say that it is nonsense for the Tory Government to be kowtowing to American multinational drug companies in a way that will result in harm, in pain and in suffering to those in our society who cannot afford it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You are against research and development. Shame on you.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Resuming debate with the Hon. Member for Edmonton East.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to stand up in favour of what the Government is endeavouring to do in passing the new Patent Act, Bill C-22.
This represents the efforts of the Government to increase the level of pharmaceutical research and development in Canada, to ensure fair prices for consumers, and to create more jobs for Canadians. What seems to be wrong with this proposal? As a pharmacist for 35 years, I believe that it is time that we started to work to get more jobs in research, more jobs for graduate pharmacists, more jobs for researchers in our universities, and in the companies that will spend more money for research and development. Among the most important of the objectives is the protection of the consumer. We have stated this over and over again. It is strange that members of the Opposition have

November 25, 1986
Patent Act
their ears plugged and their mouths working diligently trying to disprove the truth.
The Bill ensures that prices will not get out of hand by guaranteeing continued generic competition, by providing for transitional payments to the provinces, and by creating a Drug Prices Review Board. These are sound principles that are contained in this Bill. So why not deal with these one at a time?
Furthermore, by providing a more appropriate length of market protection for innovative products, the patent system will become a more effective vehicle for promoting research and development, and the transfer of technology for the benefit of all Canadians. These amendments are designed as a balanced package of measures to provide improved patent protection of pharmaceuticals, a better investment climate, and continued access by Canadians to reasonably priced drugs. It is very important that we should emphasize "reasonably priced drugs".
With the extended market exclusivity there will be expanded incentive for the creation of new employment opportunities in Canada for scientists and researchers. As a result of Bill C-22, we predict that within the next five to six years there will be up to 3,000 new high-tech jobs. High paying jobs will be created.
As a result of this legislation, there will be a reduction of Canada's dependence on technical developments in foreign countries. Why shouldn't we do this in our own country? Why shouldn't we have the pride of having our own development? The costs are not great. The costs are absolutely minimal. The public will not be obliged to pay the exorbitant prices that have been alluded to by the members of the Opposition.
The Government has received commitments from the industry, and it will increase its ratio of research and development to sales to more than double the pre-policy level by 1995. This means that the innovative sector will spend up to $1.4 billion. This is $1.4 billion in research and development over and above the amount that would have been spent otherwise. This is a commitment. With this new investment, Canada will move into the same league as Japan, Italy, and the United States. We look at these countries and say, "Why can't we be like them? Why can't we be like the Japanese and so effective, or like the Americans?" We cannot do that by piracy. We cannot do that by hiding under the covers of our supernationalistic ways of doing things. We have to be wide open and get into research and development. It is this Government's aim to develop Canadian oriented brand name drugs, to increase innovative effort and put Canada among the leaders in pharmaceutical research. I believe that this Bill is meant to achieve this goal, and it will.
For generic companies this legislation provides continued opportunities to grow and prosper. Generic drugs now marketed in Canada are unaffected by this policy. Furthermore, all existing innovative drugs now on the market will immediately be available for generic competition, provided that the generic company manufactures the fine chemical
ingredients instead of importing them. So we are looking after this area as well. To that end, all existing licences to import will be immediately extended to licences to manufacture. Licences to import and to manufacture will be available to generic drug companies wishing to export the drug.
The aim of these amendments, Mr. Speaker, is to allow pharmaceutical products to enjoy a legislative period of protection before they can be copied by the generic companies. It is important to remember that while Bill C-22 will affect the timing of the entry of new generic drugs into the market, generic companies will still have immediate access to all drugs at the end of the exclusivity period, and upon the expiry of the drug's patent.
Talking of patents, the chairman of the patents committee at the University of Alberta is the dean of pharmacy. The dean is absolutely ecstatic with our proposals. He believes that the Department of Pharmacy at the University of Alberta, as well as other departments, will benefit from this innovative Bill that we have before the House. The dean knows that he will have greater access to more researchers. He knows that the work that is being done at the university will be greatly enhanced. He knows that the University of Alberta will be contributing to the betterment of health care in Canada.
The Chairman of the patents committee has told me that there are patents waiting to be put on the market. However, no one will do that if the pirates are just around the corner ready to pounce on them. This is information from the University of Alberta. What about the other universities? New medications are not being put on the market because companies are not anxious to invest money.
Beyond the continuation of competition from the generic sector, an independent Drug Prices Review Board is to be established to ensure further fair pricing of pharmaceuticals. Under the current Patent Act, compulsory licensing has been used to generate competition to keep down prices and thus protect consumers. However, not all drugs have been copied. According to the Eastman Commission, for those which have been copied it has taken about 11.5 years after the brand name product was introduced for them to get to market. Therefore, consumers are not fully protected. With the proposed legislation the Board will widen consumer protection by looking at all prescription drug prices to determine best the fairness of the price charged to consumers.
Had the Drug Prices Review Board been in effect today, it might have looked at the prices of drugs as they have increased over the last five years. I will use the drug Beclovent as an example. In 1981, its cost was $6.60. Today, its cost is $10.90. Calculating the inflation rate at 34 per cent, it might have cost $8.84. In other words, there was a 31 per cent increase. The Drug Prices Review Board might have looked at it and asked drug companies why the price was so high. It might have asked why it had increased the price 31 per cent higher than the inflation rate over the last five years.
November 25, 1986

Another example would be the heart drug, Lanoxin. It is an inexpensive drug which is used by tens of thousands of Canadians. Its price has increased by $18 per thousand more than the inflation rate. Had the Drug Prices Review Board been in place today, it might have looked at this drug. Then there is the medicine called Dilantin which is also used by tens of thousands of Canadians. It is used for epilepsy. Its price is 185 per cent higher than the inflation rate. Surely this indicates a need to have the Drug Prices Review Board to which reference is made in Bill C-22.
According to the report of the commission of inquiry on the pharmaceutical industry, on the average, Canadian consumers pay about 80 per cent of what their American counterparts pay for the same single source drug or a drug not subject to generic competition. This is not simply the result of generic competition on a narrow range of drug products. It is evident that the bulk purchasing power of public hospitals and the power of provincial health care systems are major factors in the price differential between Canada and the United States. We can expect the trend to continue.
Dr. Harry Eastman will be heading the Drug Prices Review Board which will work in close co-operation with the provinces to ensure that drug prices continue at reasonable levels. Because of the particular interest in maintaining fair drug prices, provincial Governments will have the right to make representations in cases of alleged price abuse directly to the Board through their Ministers of health. The Board will have the power to remove patent protection from drugs priced at excessive levels.
Let us look at Nicorette. How many of us wish to quit smoking? Nicorette are for those people who have quit smoking and cannot stand the strain of not having any nicotine in their blood, so they chew it. It has risen in price by 103 per cent above the rate of inflation over the last five years. Surely it is another case for the Drug Prices Review Board. The provinces would have the right to have the Drug Prices Review Board look into drug prices.
Because the Bill changes the rules to determine exactly when a generic copy would appear on the market, it may have a short term impact upon provincial pharmacare plans which were devised without detailed knowledge of this piece of legislation. To counteract that, the Government is proposing a transitional payment of $25 million per year for the first four years of the policy. This is meant to cover any possible increases in prices which provincial Governments are not prepared to pay through their drug plans. It ultimately represents additional security for individual consumers covered by provincial plans.
Bill C-22 provides a balanced package of measures designed to fulfil a variety of objectives. It will ensure an expansion of investment in research and development. It will ensure fair prices for all drugs for Canadian consumers. It will develop new jobs and opportunities in both research and development and chemical manufacturing fields. Of course it will be to the benefit of all Canadians.
Adjournment Debate
We protect many industries. We from the West have always felt that we have tended to protect manufacturing industries which are particularly based in southern Ontario and in Quebec. In terms of the automobile industry, all Canadians pay extra money to protect jobs in southern Ontario and in Quebec. It is an obligation; it is a right. As a matter of fact, we from the West sell most of our products, if not all our natural resources, at the world price. Sometimes, as was done by the previous Government, they are sold below the world price to the detriment of those of us from the West.
I believe this piece of legislation is good for all Canadians. It will be good for the manufacture of medicines and for research and development in all areas of Canada, although it may be based particularly in eastern Canada. The West and the Atlantic provinces will experience a certain amount or a greater amount of investment in their areas.
In addition to the amendments proposed by the Government in Bill C-22 relating to the pharmaceutical area, there is a series of general amendments in the legislation. In brief, the objectives of the amendments are, first, to modify the Patent Act in order to benefit small and medium sized businesses which are the heart of job creation in Canada at this time. Why do members of the Opposition, in particular those in the NDP, say that it will be harmful to all Canadians? It will be to the benefit of all Canadians. Many more jobs will be created. It is essential that Bill C-22 be passed.
Second, they will reduce the costs Canadian inventors must pay for obtaining patents around the world by ratifying the Patent Co-operation Treaty. That is important because we live not only in a country but in a world of many countries. We must get along with them and they with us. That will be to the benefit of inventors in Canada.
Third, they will introduce a prompt and low cost method so that any interested party can request the re-examination of a patent by the Patent Office at any time during the life of the patent, rather than being obliged to suffer high litigation costs. It will also harmonize Canada's patent system with those of most other countries, making it simpler for Canadians to obtain patents abroad. This is a form of reciprocity which I believe is essential for Canadians, Canadian drug companies, researchers, chemists and pharmacists. I believe it will be to the benefit of the sick and maimed, those who require these medicines.

speechtext: The question and comment period will begin with the Hon. Member for Sudbury (Mr. Frith).

Mr. Speaker, I have listened very carefully to the points the Hon. Member has made. Would he care to explain why he as a pharmacist, from a professional standpoint, believes his Government chose to ignore the major recommendations of the Eastman Report? Why has his Government chosen to go far beyond the needs of the industry to the detriment of the consumer?

Mr. Speaker, I am afraid that the Government cannot accept the allegation that this Bill is to the detriment of all Canadians. The Bill is intended to be for the benefit of all Canadians. It will mean that we are more self-sufficient in this industry and that we increase research and development of our own medicines in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I find it curious, as I am sure any rational person would, that in defending the legislation the Government repeatedly tells us that 93 per cent of the drugs currently in the market-place will be unaffected by this legislation. If one examines that statement carefully, one finds that the Government is saying that the old legislation, since it applies to 93 per cent of the drugs on the market, is good legislation. It therefore seems ridiculous to change it, and I would like to hear the Hon. Member address that question.
I am also interested in his purported interest in the stimulation of research in Canada. As I think everyone is aware, but perhaps many Members on the government side are not, there is nothing in this legislation which guarantees that research will be carried out. We have a hope, a prayer and a promise. The Eastman Report provided a mechanism through royalties which would ensure an effective inducement to have research undertaken in Canada. Our position is that that report should
at least be subject to examination before legislation is introduced. How can the Member claim that letters, promises, hopes and prayers are better than a specific mechanism to ensure that research is done in Canada?

Mr. Speaker, we have had consultations and made arrangements with all the companies. The companies and Governments concerned have to work together. If we pass laws to cover every single agreement made, we will have nothing but laws, laws, laws. In 1969, after the previous legislation was passed, we experienced, especially in Montreal and in southern Ontario, a great loss of employment among experienced researchers. We want those jobs back. speechtext: I will recognize the Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) and the Member for Saskatoon East (Mr. Ravis) for questions and comments. We will then resume debate with the Member for Sudbury (Mr. Frith).

Mr. Speaker, it has been quite a number of years since I have worked as a pharmacist. I note that the Hon. Member who just spoke is a pharmacist and I presume he will know recent history. Under the present law, generic drugs can come on the market after the multinational corporations have had exclusive rights for four years. Under the proposed law which the Hon. Member is supporting that will take 10 years.
The price for 100 brand-name Valium tablets in Winnipeg is $15.10. The price for that amount of the generic drug is $5.64. Tagamet is used by people who have ulcers. The cost per 100 tablets of Tagamet is $39.38. The price for the generic equivalent is $15.34. One of the newest antibiotics, Amoxicillin, costs $18.25 for the brand name drug while the generic version costs $9.25.
The system which we have has brought the price of prescription drugs down to less than half of that for brand name drugs. Is that what the Hon. Member's constituents want him to vote against?
Mr. Speaker, I hear these words-
These are facts, not words.
People add two things together and get four. It just does not work that way. Of course I am in favour of lower drug prices.
You're not.

I have dispensed whatever the doctors have prescribed. When the prescription is open, we dispense the medicine which we feel is the better of the two. If it is a generic, so much the better. That saves my clients money. This will not change. All the medicines which we have today will not change at all.
Six extra years. What about the future?

We will not notice any changes. There will be only minimal changes over many, many years. However, we will provide up to 3,000 new jobs in high tech. The companies will spend $1.4 billion in investments. That will mean jobs in
Patent Act
addition to those for chemists, professors and all others who will be involved in research and development. This Bill will have absolutely no effect whatsoever, as has been stated by the Minister and the Government.

Mr. Speaker, I had the pleasure of attending a high tech conference in Saskatoon the other day. The issue of our science and technology deficit of $12.5 billion was raised there. If we were to reduce that deficit to zero, we would reduce our unemployment situation by 120,000 people, which amounts to 10 per cent of our unemployed. I am not suggesting that all of this will be done by this legislation. However, I think this legislation moves in the right direction.
There is a major university in my constituency. I was interested to read some comments in The Globe and Mail this morning by Philip Seeman, the chairman of the pharmacology department of the University of Toronto. I think this person knows what he is talking about. He says that drug designers have been packing their bags and leaving this country. He said that in recent years 19 drug companies have stopped conducting research and frozen their investments in Canada. The scare squad in the NDP is suggesting that the roofs of senior citizens will cave in on them as a result of this legislation. That is absolutely false. If there are any increases, there will be protection from them.
I know that there is a major university, the University of Alberta, in the Hon. Member's city. Does he expect that some of the spin-off contract research and development may take place at the University of Alberta as a result of this legislation? I certainly expect that that will be the case in my riding.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Member for Saskatoon East (Mr. Ravis) for that question which is very important to those of us from western Canada, particularly those of us from Saskatoon and Edmonton. My colleague is right. We cannot hide under the blanket of fear which has been thrown out by members of the Opposition, especially those in the NDP. We must move ahead and develop. This will mean great things for the University of Saskatchewan, the University of Alberta and the University of British Columbia, which has a faculty of pharmacy as well.
It is very important that we start expanding our research and development. Our scientists will be better off. We will not lose our high-tech people to other countries as we have in the past, especially after the 1969 Patent Act was passed. Over 300 such people left Montreal because there were no longer jobs for them. There will be more jobs in Saskatoon, at the University of Alberta, and in Edmonton in general. Bill C-22 is going to help provide them.

Mr. Speaker, I will preface my remarks by saying that I view with some skepticism the words which have just been mouthed by my colleagues from Saskatoon and Edmonton. Government members purport to be committed to the concept of research and development, particularly in the scientific community. The

November 25, 1986
Patent Act
Members who have just indicated their so-called support for research and development ought to look to their Minister of Science and Technology (Mr. Oberle) for solace after the debates we have had in the House of Commmons this autumn with respect to the cut-backs at the National Research Council which will affect universities across the country. However, I stray from my thesis. I will turn to a discussion of Bill C-22 which is before Parliament today.
In the next 20 minutes I hope to be able to convince my colleagues in the Conservative Party that the proposed changes to the Patent Act go too far. I hope to be able to convince my colleagues in the New Democratic Party that they should change their position as they presently support no change. To support no change flies in the face of all the debate which has ever taken place in the House of Commons. It is clear that Governments introduce legislation as a result of a need for change. That need for change is brought about by various interest groups in our society. These interest groups are often competing.
I have heard my colleagues on all sides of the House argue for the need for jobs. Who among us will oppose the creation of jobs for the youth of the country? Who among us will oppose the need for increased funds for research and development? I suspect that no one will, Mr. Speaker. Once a Government has tabled a piece of legislation, it is up to the other political Parties to determine what position they will take with respect to it. During the course of the debate on this Bill, some Members of the Conservative Party have quoted statements I have made on behalf of the Liberal Party in my capacity as health and welfare critic. As well, they have quoted other statements the source of which I frankly do not know. I wish to respond to those charges that have been made during the debate.
1 strongly believe that the Liberal Party's position on Bill C-22 can be logically and intellectually defended on the basis of the major recommendations in the report of the commission of inquiry on the pharmaceutical industry, commonly known in the political world as the Eastman Commission. Those recommendations fundamentally form the basis upon which the Liberal Party makes its position clear about the needed changes in the industry.
I want to explain why we require change to the 1969 Patent Act and I hope that the force of my logic will convince Members of the House that the Liberal Party's position is the correct one.
We accept the need for change. We accept one of the Eastman Commission's major findings that to some extent the 1969 legislation did go too far.
First, let us review the history of this subject so that all Members may have the same basis upon which to make a proper assessment of the law. The odyssey began with changes to the Patent Act in 1969. The Leader of the Opposition was
Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs at that time. After three major studies in Canada, the Government of the day decided it was time to change the Patent Act to allow more competition into the market-place. The Government of the sixties had found that the pharmaceutical manufacturers of Canada had unwarranted profit levels and unwarranted periods of exclusivity with respect to their own patents. Therefore, changes were made to the 1969 Patent Act.
I note that one of my colleagues who is in the Chamber this afternoon, the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet), was the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs responsible for the launching of the review into revisions to the 1969 Patent Act. He established the Eastman Commission which, I submit, must be the foundation upon which any Government must base the change, the purpose and direction of the 1969 law. Surely no one can argue that the Eastman Commission represents the largest source of inquiry into the impact of the 1969 laws on the pharmaceutical industry, the research and development, and its impact on job opportunities for our university graduates.
In summary, the Eastman Commission Report represents the state of the art in information with respect to the pharmaceutical industry in Canada today.
I want to refer to some of the major findings of the Eastman Report. For example, he found that the 1969 Patent Act amendment has not, as expected, been detrimental to the profitability of large multinationals. In fact, he found that the profitability in the pharmaceutical industry exceeds every other industry within the major sectors of the Canadian economy. In terms of growth, he found that there has been no difference in growth in job opportunities between the pharmaceutical industry in Canada and that of the United States.
I think we do a disservice to the debate to use the rhetoric of anti-American sentiment. I do not think it does much to advance the quality or intellectual raison d'etre of the Bill. Second, I will not resort to using examples of drugs that have become completely outpriced in Canada because it also clouds the decision-making that must occur with respect to Bill C-22.
The Government of the day introduces a Bill before the Parliament of Canada because it believes there is a need for change as a result of the competing interests that are subject to that legislation. The concern is, to what extent is change necessary in the industry?
I believe the only way we can properly assess the need for change is to base it on the recommendations of the Eastman Commission. Let us use research and development credits as an example. Conservative Members in particular argue that this Bill is necessary because it will allow a tremendous increase in the amount of money that the pharmaceutical industry will commit to research and development in this country. I would assume, therefore, that they anticipate that more jobs will be created for graduates from our universities, providing meaningful employment in their area of expertise in the scientific community. Eastman said that we should be
November 25, 1986

increasing the royalties that are paid to the pharmaceutical manufacturers in Canada from 4 per cent to 14 per cent, to create a very large pool of research and development funds that would be allocated back to the pharmaceutical manufacturers on the basis of their R and D commitment in this country. I will deal with research and development more specifically later.
I indicated that the Eastman Commission found that there was no effect on the profitability of that sector, and that the 1969 legislation had in fact saved consumers in this country $256 million per annum. One must respect the findings of the Eastman Commission after 18 to 24 months of intensive study of the industry. It is important to note what is said about the 1969 legislation. Let me quote the following from page 30 of the Eastman Report:
Despite the considerable achievements of these policies, the Commission recommends some major modifications and extensions. The process leading to authorization for marketing should become more rapid and more consultative.
In other words, despite those major findings, he recommended modifications and change. That is why I am fundamentally opposed to the position taken by members of the New Democratic Party. They should realize that the recommendations of a commission of this importance which studied the results of the 1969 legislation should be seriously considered by every major political Party. Eastman goes on to state:
This modified Canadian system for the pharmaceutical industry would make Canada a more attractive site for pharmaceutical production and research.
I have no qualms about that at all. He says:
The relative attraction of Canada for the industry compared to other countries will increase further in the foreseeable future because of the growing trend for Governments of most industrially advanced countries to interfere directly and forcefully in the activities of the pharmaceutical industry.
He goes on to point out that in his opinion Canada is not well placed to become a major world centre for pharmaceutical research or for the production of active chemical ingredients. That is very important because the Liberal Party's position on the pharmaceutical legislation reflects the major findings of the Eastman Commission. That is why the Liberal Party takes the following position: It supports the introduction of a four-year period of exclusivity for patent holding firms during which time a generic company would be precluded from obtaining a licence to import, coupled with a hefty royalty increase, amounting to approximately 14 per cent of a licencee's sales which would be paid into a pharmaceutical royalty fund and returned to the pharmaceutical manufacturers of Canadian members, according to the amount of R and D undertaken in Canada.
I am suggesting that this Bill goes too far in looking after the interests of the pharmaceutical manufacturers of Canada, and does not go far enough in protecting the needs of the consumers in this country. Clearly, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) either does not understand the Bill or is deliberately hiding from Canadians the effects of this Bill on manufacturing and pharmacy prescription prices in Canada.
Patent Act
If we were to take the Consumer and Corporate Affairs Minister at his own word when he says that the cost of drugs will not change by one penny, why is it that his own Bill has provision for $100 million in transitory payments, $25 million a year, which will be given to the provincial Ministries of Health to cushion the impact which this proposed legislation will have on provincial Governments which have the constitutional responsibility for the delivery of pharmacare? I submit that the Minister knows full well that he is simply playing with definitions, that in fact this Bill will increase the cost of drugs to consumers and will have an impact on provincial Treasuries as well through the Ministry of Health expenditures.
For the life of me, I do not understand why the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs simply does not say it is going to have that effect. He defends it on the basis of the need for change so we can have greater opportunities for our young people coming out of universities and more commitment toward research and development. The point I am making is, how can a Government, after accepting the report of a commission, which is one of the most widely respected with respect to the pharmaceutical industry in Canada, totally ignore the major recommendations of its report and go far and beyond the recommendations?
The Eastman recommendations, in my opinion, represent a balanced view between the needs of the industry, which I believe are legitimate, and the consumer. I have listened to my colleagues from the Province of Quebec who have eloquently argued the need for a change to the pharmaceutical Act so that there can be some degree of job protection for the Provinces of Quebec and Ontario which, to some extent, is the heart of the pharmaceutical industry. I accept that argument from my colleagues from Quebec. In addition, I accept the argument from my colleagues from all three political Parties in the House about the need for more commitment to research and development. That can be attained just as easily by accepting the recommendations of the Eastman Commission as it can by implementing the law being proposed under Bill C-22.
Clearly our position, as a Liberal Party, is somewhat between the position taken by the New Democratic Party and that taken by the Conservatives. The question is, which one of us is correct? That will be at the heart of the debate. I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that I have accepted the determination of the Eastman Commission that Canada is not well placed to become a major world centre for pharmaceutical research and for the production of active chemical ingredients. However, we could increase the royalty funds on generics from 4 per cent to 14 per cent and could in effect create a sizeable fund for research and devlopment, perhaps not as a world class centre, which is the point today's Government is making, but certainly it would aid in the creation of jobs for our young people in the pharmaceutical industry and in the scientific community.
Where I find it difficult to accept the argument is that the Government had to go beyond the recommendation of the

November 25, 1986
Patent Act
Eastman Commission to the point where it almost doubled the degree of exclusivity recommended by the Commission. In addition, I must confess I have some difficulty with the Eastman Commission accepting the position of the Chairman of the Drug Prices Review Board. It seems odd to me that the Conservative Party, which came to power with the philosophy of deregulation, is now bringing forward a piece of legislation which is going to complicate the pharmaceutical industry. It is going to put into effect another layer of bureaucracy and regulatory mechanisms in order to ensure that consumers are not going to be ripped off by this law. If the Government was concerned about the consumers, why did it not just simply implement the recommendations of the Eastman Commission?
The Eastman Commission's recommendations would have allowed better opportunities for the pharmaceutical industry, yet it would have gone a lot further in protection of consumer affairs without the need to resort to a regulatory mechanism than what is represented in this law.
I therefore appeal to my colleagues on all political fronts that when this Bill does finally manage to go to committee, we will be allowed the fullest opportunity to call witnesses. I want to find out from those witnesses whether or not they agree with the recommendations made in Bill C-22, as proposed by the Conservative Government, or if they are more in favour of a balanced view represented by the recommendations of the Eastman Commission. I believe very strongly that intellectually the arguments which have been marshalled by the Eastman Commission could be used to represent a balanced view for the needs of consumers and for the industry. As I said earlier, I respect the needs of the industry, but I happen to disagree that it requires 10 years of exclusivity to achieve its goals and aims.
Finally, I suspect that the reason the pharmaceutical manufacturers of Canada have hurried to such a great degree in pressuring the Government for the implementation of Bill C-22 is not only tied up, to some extent, in the free trade negotiations with the United States, a fact I view as deplorable, but that, in addition, the 1969 legislation, coupled with the changes recommended by the Eastman Commission, would have become a model piece of legislation in other jurisdictions throughout the western world. That, I believe, is at the heart of the matter. What the pharmaceutical manufacturers of Canada fear most is not the impact the Canadian legislation has on their percentage of world-wide sales but the impact the Canadian legislation would have if enacted by European countries or by consumer advocates in the United States. What they fear most is the impact of the 1969 Patent Act in other jurisdictions.
In conclusion, I believe we should look at how best the Canadian Parliament could serve the needs of consumers, the needs of the pharmaceutical industry, the needs of the young to have access to jobs in the scientific community, and the need for jobs. I submit that what we should be doing is bringing forward a piece of legislation which reflects the major recommendations of the Eastman Commission and not the legislation proposed by the Conservative Government.

Mr. Speaker, I want to ask the Hon. Member for Sudbury (Mr. Frith) several questions. He referred to the 1969 legislation passed by the Liberal Government when the present Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) was the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. The Hon. Member said, and he knows, that it worked very well. It saved the people of Canada tens of millions of dollars. Why, then, was it necessary to open up the whole question? An article which appeared in the August-September issue of This Magazine, written by John Sawatsky, goes over the history of what happened. Mr. Sawatsky gives as the reason the fact that Liberal Members of Parliament were putting the pressure first on the then Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet), and then on the following Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, the former Hon. Member for Nickel Belt, and she appointed Professor Eastman mainly to neutralize the pressures she was getting from Liberal Members of Parliament. I am sure the Hon. Member for Sudbury has read this article, and I would like him to comment. Mr. Sawatsky is talking about discussions which went on last June about the former Bill. He wrote:
Then, behind the speaker's chair on the floor of the Commons, Cote quietly met with Liberal MP Doug Frith, a Sudbury pharmacist who serves as his party's caucus chairman and critic on social policy. They cut a deal in which Frith agreed not to oppose Cote's interim legislation. The Conservative-Liberal agreement suddenly made temporary legislation politically viable. "Only the NDP will bitch," they agreed.
That is a very serious charge. Finally, I want to put to the Hon. Member that we are not debating Professor Eastman's recommendations.
You want no change?
On the contrary. If the Government had brought in a Bill based on Professor Eastman's recommendations-
Oh, good.
-we could have discussed those recommendations.
That's what I wanted to hear.

But we are not debating that. If and when the Government brings in that type of legislation, we will look at it clause by clause and probably support a good part of it. But that is not what we are debating. What we are debating is a Bill which gives the multinational corporations just about everything they want. That is why we are opposing it.

Mr. Speaker, I believe I should probably begin my response by asking a question. I find it passing strange that the New Democratic Party finally admits that it would be in favour of a Bill which would reflect the findings of the Eastman Commission. That does not differ at all from the position of the Liberal Party, a position I have taken consistently throughout the last two years. I have listened to my
November 25, 1986

colleagues from the Province of Quebec who have legitimate concerns about the impact of the 1969 legislation on the pharmaceutical industry in their province.
The so-called secret deal that was made behind the Speaker's chair is simply this. The Minister of the day was finding out whether or not we would be amenable to the recommendations made by the Eastman Commission. I say it publicly to Ministers opposite that if they wish to amend this legislation to reflect the major recommendations of the Eastman Commission then we would not be in full debate in this Elouse on this particular legislation today.
I also wish to indicate to my colleague from Winnipeg why it was that the former Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs established the Eastman Commission in the first place. The establishment of the Commission came about as a result of a request made at a federal-provincial conference held in the early part of the 1980s signed by every one of the provincial Ministers which indicated that they wanted to have an inquiry into the pharmaceutical industry established because of their concern about the impact of the 1969 legislation on research and development levels in Canada. The then Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, the Hon. Member for Papineau, acceded to the request.
As I have indicated before, I think the Eastman inquiry represents the highest state of information that we can possibly attain in Canada with respect to the state of the pharmaceutical industry. My Conservative colleagues opposite would do well to change their minds with respect to the proposed legislation.
[ Translation]

Mr. Speaker, may I say that I fail to understand why today, after so many years, the Liberals still do not realize they made a mistake when they passed legislation which did not protect our drug research and researchers. At the time, we the people of Montreal could predict that tens of thousands of jobs would be lost, and today we can still see the empty buildings vacated by companies which did drug research. They are responsible for this and during those seven years they did not have the courage to backtrack and introduce the kind of legislation we are advocating today.
I can appreciate the position of the New Democratic Party, with their socialist approach and conviction that the Government should control everything. But I do not understand the Liberal Party, they are supposed to be in favour of liberalization. It is very difficult to understand. Why should this debate last so long? Why so much protest to make the debate last as long as possible and to mislead people?
Should we have more unemployed or people who can afford to pay for drugs? That is the main issue. What are we going to do with unemployed people if they cannot pay for drugs? The best thing is to have people with money to pay for them. That is the point.
My question is simple. Why didn't the Liberals, why didn't your party have the courage to table a Bill as sound and well
Patent Act
drafted as the one we are tabling today? Why not say: Yes, we will let people invest in research and development and at the same time, we will control prices in the long term? Why don't you agree with this position?
Because, Mr. Speaker, we are not stupid.
Hear, hear.

I think the Hon. Member is mistaken in his allegations about unemployment in this industry. After examining the issue for eighteen months, the Eastman Commission found that the 1969 legislation did not affect the employment situation in the industry, and Mr. Speaker, I think that if the Conservatives want a higher level of research and development in this country, it would be much easier to change the royalty system in the industry, as recommended by the Eastman Commission, by increasing royalties by 14 per cent. To me, Mr. Speaker, this would be much easier and more effective than the legislation we have now.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a brief comment with respect to the speech of the Hon. Member for Sudbury (Mr. Frith) and, in particular, in response to a question raised by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow).
This Party has certainly long fought for an affordable health care system. It was never our position back in 1982 or in 1983 that the provisions that were brought in in 1969 to deal with what were some of the highest drug prices in the world should in fact be changed in the absence of compelling evidence that there could be significant improvements, both in the quality of drugs offered to Canadians as well as enhanced research, without jeopardizing the prices paid by consumers.
Certainly, if one is given a choice between the Draconian proposals put forward by the Government and the provisions of the Eastman Report, then clearly the Eastman Report is preferable. I wish to make it clear, speaking as one Member of Parliament, and I know I speak on behalf of my colleagues on this point, that I am not satisfied that the very high levels of profits of the multinational corporations in the drug field should be further enhanced by any changes to the 1969 compulsory licensing legislation.

In conclusion, I rest my case. I began my treatise this afternoon hoping that I could convince some of my colleagues that the Eastman Commission's recommendations were the route to follow. I have now found during the debate, and I appreciate it very much, that my colleagues from the New Democratic Party now admit, as the Liberal Party does, that the Eastman Commission represents the direction to follow in terms of the pharmaceutical industry in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I would like to express my personal satisfaction with the tabling of this Bill by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) I also want to take this opportunity to mention the support received from the Federation de I'Age d'Or du Quebec. The president of the Association, Mrs. Rose-Aimee Leblanc, sent a letter to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, and I would like to quote some passages from this letter:
On behalf of the Federation de I'Age d'Or du Quebec, I would like to reiterate our support as expressed on many occasions for the changes in the Patent Act announced by the Government. The Federation de I'Age d'Or du Quebec is agreeable to having an adequate period of exclusivity guaranteed for new drugs.
The present legislation is unfair and discriminates against researchers and scientific experts in the pharmaceutical industry, because it denies them the protection enjoyed by other industrial sectors and by researchers in other countries.
We are convinced that these changes in the Patent Act are necessary to stimulate research and find discover new drugs to treat diseases for which a cure has yet to be found such as cancer, Alzheimer's disease, AIDS and various cardio-vascular diseases.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to get back to the pride Canadians feel in what they do and their pride in the quality of their products, and to how important it is for Canadians to be involved in pharmaceutical R & D.
The purpose of the Bill before the House today is to ensure that consumers will pay reasonable prices for drugs and that the pharmaceutical industry will meet its commitments to engage in research and development, and we see these two objectives as the primary objectives of the new legislation. To ensure these objectives are achieved, the new policy provides for establishing an independent Board that will review drug prices and monitor investments by the drug companies. The Board will have a very important role. The Review Board will consist of five members, and will be chaired by Dr. Harry Eastman himself, who is a professor in the Department of Economic Science at the University of Toronto. Dr. Eastman was chairman of the Commission everyone is talking about today which submitted its report in May 1985. All members of the Board will be appointed by the Governor in Council for a period of five years and may be reappointed for one further year. Members must be persons without any interests in the pharmaceutical sector. I think this guarantees that hearings held by the Board will be used to hear the complaints or requests of consumers. The Minister may also, if he so wishes, establish an advisory panel to be composed of members of the various groups concerned, which will advise the Minister with respect to the appointments of members of the Board. I think that is also a useful addition.
To guarantee that drug prices will be fair, every patentee of a invention shall provide the Board with information on the prices of patented medicines manufactured or sold by the patentee. To determine whether drug prices are excessive, the Board must consider factors such as the consumer price
index-if there are price increases in other sectors, there may also be increases in the pharmaceutical sector-the price of such products in other countries, which is also an important factor, the price of similar drugs in Canada and, if necessary, we could go even further, the cost of making and marketing drugs and such other factors that in the opinion of the Board are relevant. When the Board's experts indicate that a given price is excessive, the Board will establish a maximum. If a company persists in selling the product at a price above the established maximum, the Board may, after holding public hearings, rescind the period of protection against imports of generic equivalents or the manufacturing thereof. Furthermore, the Board may rescind the period of protection granted for other drugs produced by the company. I may recall that although public hearings will be held, the Government's purpose is to keep procedures simple and to hand down decisions as quickly as possible.
The Board will be working in close co-operation with the provinces. We are all aware of the interest the provinces have in drug prices. Provincial Health Ministers will have the right to appear before the Board and explain their position.
Public participation is also important since the public can advise the Board of any case of allegedly excessive prices. In certain cases, investigations will result directly from inquiries from the public, while at the present time, members of the public have no idea to whom they should complain. The hearings held by the Board will not constitute an exclusive forum for the pharmaceutical companies. The general public will be able to attend.
The Bill also grants real powers to the Review Board. This will enable the Board to offer greater price protection than is now possible. Many drugs have no competition from generic products. Consumers therefore have no idea if they are paying a reasonable price for these products. I think that we all know that, only 7 per cent of all prescription drugs now have a generic equivalent. This means that there is no generic equivalent for 93 per cent of all prescription drugs and that it is therefore impossible to verify the prices of these products. The Board will be responsible for reviewing the prices of all drugs now being sold to determine whether the consumer is paying a fair price or not.
The Board will also review the price of drugs well before generic equivalents are available. This is also an important factor. The Board will put pressure on companies to lower prices as soon as the drugs appear on the market. This is another major improvement over the situation which has existed since 1969. Today, prices go down only when a generic product comes on the market. From now on, the Board will be able to determine as soon as a product is put on the market whether its price is excessive and ask that it be lowered. Consumers will not have to wait for a generic product to come on the market to benefit from competitive prices.

generics, there is absolutely no competition on the level of prices. The Board, therefore, will have to protect consumers both during this period and following the introduction of generics.

He said: Mr. Speaker, as the motion indicates, I have presented to the House of Commons Bill C-234 respecting the search for missing children. This Bill was presented on a previous occasion to the House of Commons. It has been widely discussed among those interested in the subject of missing children.
I wish to advise you of the reason that I seek approval for this Bill on second reading. For many years in the municipalities and across each of the provinces, the problem of missing children has caused great consternation and difficulties, not only to the parents of missing children, but to the authorities that under our social system are responsible for young persons.
The provinces, through their legislative assemblies and their Governments, have been unable to provide a suitable solution to the problem of missing children. For this reason, I attempted to draft in a Bill suitable for passage through the Parliament of Canada, a solution to the problem of missing children. It is important that Parliament understand that it does have jurisdiction in this matter. Heretofore it has been considered that the problem of missing children was the concern of the provincial Governments and the legislative authorities of the separate provinces.
However, I wish to point out to the House of Commons that Parliament has already taken responsibility with respect to children under the age of 16 years. In Section 197 of the Criminal Code it is made very clear that every parent, foster parent, or guardian of a child under the age of 16 years is under a legal duty to provide the necessities of life to that child.
In order to perform and implement that obligation under the Criminal Code, it follows that as part of our criminal law jurisdiction we should provide a parent or guardian with the method to ensure that the child remains under their care and

November 25, 1986
Missing Children Search Act
control, in order that they can perform their legal duty. It is under that authority that I drafted and presented to this House as a Private Members' Bill, Bill C-234, which has the short title Missing Children Search Act. I will just state briefly, because I have indicated the contents of the Bill on other occasions, that the Bill is to authorize a parent to in turn give authority to a police officer to search for a missing child, that is, a child under the age of 16 years.
What is important is not that we regard the specific provisions and words of this Bill, but that we grasp the subject matter of it, and recognize that there is a huge problem. The Parliament of Canada, if it has any legislative authority, should exercise it in favour of a resolution of the problem. Even if the House does not see fit to give second reading to this Bill and reference to a legislative committee, I would be more than content if the House of Commons would see fit to refer the subject matter of this Bill to an appropriate committee. I think the appropriate committee would be the Standing Committee on Justice and Solicitor General. However, I will leave that to the determination of the House.
I wish to make a couple of remarks that very graphically bring to the attention of the House of Commons and the Canadian public the concerns that have resulted in the introduction of this Bill.
When I first introduced this legislation in the House of Commons, I made the statement that police forces across Canada could tell you whether your motor vehicle was stolen or missing, but they did not keep any record of missing children. I was challenged on that point. Unfortunately, it was true. Since then the Solicitor General has directed the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to add missing children to its CPIC register. To a certain extent, the problem has now been resolved.
I wish to present some other facts so that Members will know the extent of this problem. Of the 11 children whom Clifford Olson admitted killing, only one was a subject of a police search. That is the extent of the difficulties that arise from police involvement in searches for missing children. I am trying to bridge that gap and bring parents and the police together, so that missing children will be found and a search will be conducted immediately.
In the few moments I have at my disposal, I wish to say that there have been many people who have concerned themselves and made it almost a career to deal with the problem of missing children. I mentioned Judy Cullen, with whom I have had a number of discussions. I also wish to refer to Mr. and Mrs. Gary Rosenfeldt, who have been crusaders in this field. We all owe them a debt of gratitude.
I wish to present to the Parliament of Canada, and the people of Canada, one case which I think typifies the problem. It is the case of Jeffrey Murray, who went missing in January of 1986 from his home in the Halifax-Dartmouth area of Nova Scotia. Ten months later this 14-year-old boy was still missing.
I wish to quote the following from a media account of Jeffrey Murray's situation:
At first RCMP, treating Jeffrey's disappearance as a runaway case, did receive tips there were a few local sightings of Jeffrey, but they were unable to track him down.
Finally, Mrs. Murray and her husband Robert,
-made the difficult decision of signing Jeffrey's guardianship to the province, giving police power to arrest their son and bring him home.
That is a very poor solution, Mr. Speaker, to a very real human problem. In order to receive police assistance and empower the police to search for one's own child, a parent in the Province of Nova Scotia-and it is the same in most of the other provinces in Canada-has to in effect make a complaint that his or her child is a delinquent and that they require public assistance by way of guardianship. That is the solution that the provincial legislators have provided. It is not a good enough solution. If the Parliament of Canada in the exercising of its authority under the Constitution of Canada can provide a better solution, then I think that we should at least explore it.
I have suggested the device of a parent being able to authorize the police to make a search. That is one suggestion. There may be better suggestions. I would be the first to recognize a better form. What there has to be in any solution to the problem is the ability of parents to enlist very quickly the aid of the police forces in their community and across Canada in the search for a missing child. Why should they do that? It is because it has been established time and time again that runaways or children who leave their homes and go missing become almost inevitably the victims of crime. Anyone, including the Solicitor General (Mr. Kelleher) if that is his position, who tells me that there is not a connection between missing children and the criminal law of Canada simply does not know what he or she is talking about. Missing children become, almost in every case, victims of violence or victims of crime. In the best of cases they are simply inducted into a world of outlaws in society; they become outlaws. If we visit major urban areas across Canada, we see graphic evidence in this regard on every main street from Halifax to Vancouver including St. John's, Newfoundland.
We are trying to respond to a real problem. The solutions may not be perfect, but at least it is a start. I enlist the assistance of all Hon. Members of the House in attempting to determine a course of action which can be taken under the laws of Canada to resolve this very serious social problem.
