I believe very strongly that the problem of missing children in Canada is the type of issue where we can all set aside any partisan concerns we may have and work together to develop some effective legislation or an effective solution to the problem.
Again I congratulate the Hon. Member. Indeed, I commend the Government for some of its actions on this important subject over the course of its mandate.
As we know, the former Solicitor General announced in December, 1985 several initiatives to address the particular problem of missing children. For example, it was announced that there would be a central registry on missing children. The press release indicated that the RCMP would be creating a central registry in Ottawa to assist police forces and concerned agencies across Canada in locating and identifying missing children. Also it indicated that the registry would be linked with the Canadian Police Information Centre which had online terminals in almost all police departments in Canada. It would also be linked with similar information systems in the United States and through Interpol to the rest of the world. The plans were to have the registry operational by July, 1986.
As I speak this afternoon, I am not clear on whether or not the central registry is fully operational. However, I believe it is a step in the right direction. I think the Government is truly concerned about the particular issue.
As the Hon. Member for Halifax West pointed out, there is no national legislation in Canada to deal with the problem of missing children. There is such legislation in the United States. Mr. Speaker, as I am sure you are aware, over 2,000 children are reported missing every year in Canada. It is a large number of children. The Canadian police information computer usually has an accurate record of the number of missing children. Of course the 2,000 figure is an estimate. At any given moment in time there are approximately 2,000 missing children. While the CPIC usually has an accurate record of the number of missing children, as I understand it the circumstances of their disappearance are not included in that computer. At times we are told that police departments may enter incomplete descriptions or conflicting information.
Missing children fall into three categories-runaways, stranger abductions, and parental abductions. Contrary to popular belief, most police departments do not wait a prescribed period of time, for example 24 hours, before recording a child is missing. My information is that generally police departments treat each case individually, taking into consideration factors such as whether the child is known to be a runaway or whether there are feuding parents and parental abduction is likely. At times precious little can be done with
Missing Children Search Act
regard to a missing child when there is parental abduction. Of course there are stranger abductions. They are of paramount concern. It is an offence under the Criminal Code of Canada.
As well, when we are dealing with runaways, while some children may rebel and decide to run away from home, we know that at times they all too often fall into the hands of certain degenerate elements in society and begin a life of crime, whether it be prostitution or drug peddling. There are those individuals in society who decide to use runaways. Of course runaways are very vulnerable to exploitation by different people in society.
We all know that Canadian corporations are eager to become involved in the search for missing children. Many corporations in Canada are prepared to offer financial assistance. However, I believe the bottom line is that the Government of Canada and we as parliamentarians have a responsibility to ensure that as a Parliament we do whatever we can to ensure that the problem is dealt with. While the Government of Canada has taken certain initiatives for which I commend it, I do not believe we have gone far enough.
There is now a central registry on missing children. The Government has declared a National Missing Children Day on May 25 of each year. Pilot studies are being initiated in different Canadian cities. I believe, as does the Hon. Member for Halifax West, that there is a need for national legislation. At the very least, there is a need for the subject to be debated and discussed at the national level here in the Parliament of Canada through the Standing Committee on Justice and Solicitor General. Once the matter is referred to that particular committee, the committee will have the opportunity to invite various groups and individuals in society to come forward, such as the Canadian Centre for Missing Children. That is a voluntary organization in Edmonton. I would like to commend it publicly for the work it has done concerning missing children. In particular I would like to congratulate it for the literature it has produced on the subject. I believe it is doing some very fine work and I would like to hear from its representatives. I would like them to come to the committee to discuss their concerns so we as parliamentarians can decide how to deal with this national problem.
As the Hon. Member pointed out, the issue should be addressed by the Parliament of Canada. While different provincial Governments are discussing and dealing with it, we have to recognize that the problem is national in scope. When children go missing they often cross provincial borders. Therefore, we have a need for national legislation.
I have some technical concerns regarding this Bill. I have asked the Library of Parliament to review the legislation and provide me with a report on its potential legal problems. I want to present to this House as many times as I have the opportunity the subject of missing children.
It is to his credit that he has persevered.
We can all relate to the sense of anguish and despair faced by the parent of a child who has disappeared. We can relate to the frustration and anger they feel when they believe that perhaps the police have not responded as quickly as they should have. We can understand and empathize with those who are angry with the fact that in many cases when a child is abducted and taken out of the country, the parent in question is in effect told there is no possible way of dealing with that abduction.
There are three different forms of child abduction that we deal with under the general scope of this Bill. The first is the child who chooses to run away. The second is the child abducted by a parent. The third is a child abducted by strangers. It is very difficult indeed to know what sort of numbers we are dealing with. We are certainly talking about hundreds and hundreds of children. For example, as of January, 1984, over 1,200 children between the ages of 10 and 16 went missing. An additional 160 under the age of 10 were also missing. I suspect those figures under-represent the extent of the problem. However, what is clearly beyond the shadow of a doubt is that this Parliament must recognize there is a problem and that the subject matter should be studied by the committee.
I want to join with my colleagues in commending the initiatives taken by the former Solicitor General, the Hon. Member for Wellington-Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Beatty), in this area. Approximately one year ago he announced the creation of a central registry on missing children, a Canadian information centre on missing children, and the establishment of a National Missing Children's Day, as well as consultation through a national conference on this whole question. Those are all important initiatives. It is also important not to lose sight of the fact that while legislative structures are important, we have to examine why children are running away. Too often these children are fleeing from absolutely intolerable conditions at home. They run away as a last resort. Certainly we as a society have to recognize the problem and examine responses. Too many children are fleeing from abuse, whether it be sexual, physical or phsychological. I suggest that it is essential to put in place the resources necessary to deal with the problem. Legislation on the subject of sexual abuse of young children is now before Parliament. As a member of the legislative committee studying that problem, I know we look forward to improvements being made to the legislation, both in its definition of offences and in improving the ability of young children to communicate their story in court.
I also believe that while it is important to look at the legal structure, the committee dealing with this subject must also call witnesses to give evidence about why children in larger and larger numbers are leaving their homes. We have to examine, for example, the question of violence in the family. We have to ask ourselves, as I said during the debate on Bill C-15, whether we are prepared to continue to tolerate a provision of the Criminal Code which allows children to be beaten by their parents or guardians. We have to ask ourselves if perhaps the time has not come to move beyond that, as has been done already in Sweden.
I want to commend the groups which have been active in this area. They have been vocal and they have put incredible energy into dealing with this problem, often at great personal expense. I think of, for example, the group known as Mothers Against Abduction and Mcrder. This is a group of mothers who in many cases have experienced personally the tragedy of the loss of a child. Sharon Rosenfeldt, the mother of one of the victims of Clifford Olson, is active in this group as well as in Victims of Violence and with the Canadian Centre for Missing Children. I believe we owe a debt to the organizations, and the individuals who work so hard within them, which have helped push this matter. Today it will be referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Solicitor General.

In addition to the subject matter of this Bill, I hope the committee will consider very seriously the preventive

measures which society must take to ensure that our most precious resource, our children, are not in a situation of having to flee or being subject to abduction.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to join with my colleagues today during Private Members' Hour to discuss the Bill and the amendment to it. There are four things which I think are very serious in Canadian society. They are drug and alcohol abuse, child abuse, pornography, and missing children. I believe that these four things are attacking the social fabric of our society. I commend the Member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby) for the efforts he has made to ensure that this Private Member's Bill will be referred to the appropriate committee.
In the past, the tragedy of missing children only came to our attention through the media. Today there is a greater awareness of missing children through pictures in bus shelters, post offices and newspapers. I have even included them in my quarterly householder to my constituents.
Today, in addition to the Bill, I want to dwell on the vital part which the community can play in the tragic saga of missing children. Community volunteers aid in the search for children and in educating parents and children to try to prevent child abduction and runaways. I would like to speak about a program in my constituency which I think presents a partial solution to this problem. Governments at all levels must work with our volunteer agencies. The program All About Me ID was commenced in Saskatoon a couple of years ago. It was shown on national television about a year ago. The objectives of the program are to provide an accurate and complete description and identification of children and, perhaps more important, to educate parents and children about preventing abduction.
The All About Me ID program started in March, 1985, in Saskatoon with a massive volunteer effort co-ordinated by Saskatoon media and Child Find Saskatchewan. With the help of hundreds of volunteers and retired RCMP officers, and with donations from many corporations and volunteer organizations, this program was put into place. Approximately 45,000 passports were issued to Saskatoon school children in a major campaign. That includes a large majority of the school-aged children in our city. The program also registered 17,000 children in the rural areas surrounding Saskatoon. I am pleased that there has already been a decrease in the number of cases reported to the police.
As you are probably aware, Mr. Speaker, each year in the neighbourhood of 1,000 to 1,200 children go missing. While many of those children have only forgotten to call home while they are out after school with playmates, last year five children were never found. As far as I am concerned, that is five too many.
The All About Me ID program is also under way in Prince Albert where over 7,000 children have already been registered. Plans are under way to implement the program in Calgary. I learned today that a radio station there has undertaken to give
Missing Children Search Act
the program a boost, much as it received in Saskatoon. The campaign is also under way in the Province of Quebec. In Saskatoon all costs associated with the production of the passports were borne by volunteer and service groups in the city. At present the passports cost approximately $1.50 each.
I do not have a copy of a passport with me, but it is basically a piece of paper about eight inches by 11 inches folded three ways. Inside it has a picture, fingerprints, and all vital statistics pertinent to the particular child. The passport is the property of parents who make it available to police in the event the child goes missing. Of course, the fingerprints and picture become the key elements of the passport.
With the enactment of the Bill currently before the House, police agencies across the country would be brought in to assist in the search for missing children. The All About Me ID passport will be of great assistance in the search. By providing police with ready-made identification and vital fingerprints the All About Me ID program eliminates a burden for them and puts the search in motion much sooner. Time is always of the essence in abduction cases where the trail grows cold very quickly.
The All About Me ID program has a preventive component as well. There is a list of 12 precautions contained in the passport. They may appear to be pretty basic, but I believe they cause many children to go missing. For example, never leave a child unattended. Remind children never to talk to strangers or accept candy from them. Make sure children know the telephone numbers for their home and for the police station. Encourage children to tell parents of encounters which are threatening to them. Tell children to go to Child Find if the worst happens. Help can be found there. I think the Child Find organization is one of the better known national organizations with agencies in every city.
The Bill before the House today is of vital importance to the well-being of all Canadian children. When my hon. colleague introduced the Bill for first reading in March, 1985, he stressed that this Bill "would ensure the assistance of police officers and searchers and encourage the participation of other agencies and the public". It is high time this action was taken. My own City of Saskatoon has proven that a co-ordinated effort of volunteer agencies can provide an invaluable service to the police. This type of action would occur on a nation-wide basis with the enactment of this Bill. Both the City of Saskatoon police and Child Find Saskatchewan feel that they have an excellent working relationship which is of great benefit in the searches for missing children.
By enacting this Bill we must not assume that the entire burden of finding children who tragically go missing will fall on police agencies. They already have limited resources and manpower. We would be defeating the noble and vital purpose of this Bill if we strained those resources by placing the full responsibility of search and find on the law enforcement agencies. Through this Bill my colleague intended to encourage joint participation by families, communities, volunteer organizations and law enforcement agencies across the

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to say a few words on this very important matter in Bill C-234. As Members know, the Government is very cognizant of its responsibilities in this very important social issue and has already taken concrete steps to put in place legislation and procedures to deal with this matter. Certainly more remains to be done, and, as in other areas of government responsibility, this important social issue requires regular review to ensure that the legislation and procedures of the day remain effective and appropriate.
It would be very gratifying if some single Act of Parliament, some specific piece of legislation which we could all support, would deal with the problem in a comprehensive and effective way. Unhappily, this is not the case. The matter is complex, touches on many social issues, and invokes a host of legal views and constitutional principles that are very often conflicting in nature.
We are all aware of the pain and the grief to the parent or guardian and other family members, the injury or hurt to the missing child himself or herself, when these unfortunate events occur.
Children absent themselves from their homes or residences for a variety of reasons. Sometimes it is forcibly, sometimes voluntarily. All tools at hand must be employed to determine the whereabouts of a missing child, and, where appropriate, return that child to its home. Obviously, our various police forces can and must play a significant role in the location process. Effective federal legislation is an important part of the formula. Heavy handed legislation, on the other hand, can only give birth to endless litigation and is counterproductive.
Bill C-234 contains several clauses which give me considerable difficulty. I very much hope that the appropriate committee will consider some of these clauses closely when it has the opportunity to do so. In particular, I single out Clause 7(3) which states:
When a warrant is reported in respect of a missing child, the parent of the child or any police officer or member of a police department may enter and search any place or premises as though the warrant was a warrant to search for the child issued under the Criminal Code of Canada.
1 am confident that every member of the House, as would any normal thinking member of Canadian society, would have every sympathy for a parent or guardian searching frantically
for a missing child and would, in most conceivable circumstances, co-operate willingly in the search. However, to enact legislation which gives the right of search of private property by a parent or guardian without any reasonable control or limitation seems to me to fly in the face of many of the protections accorded private citizens under the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. A distraught adult, at whatever the hour, day or night, brandishing a piece of paper and demanding his or her right to search my home or business, would give me pause for thought. Who is this person, how credible is his or her story, what abuses to my security or privacy are put at risk by giving free entry? How am I to know, how is some elderly widow or anyone else to know, whether the warrant, assuming the claimant has produced such a piece of paper, is valid or legal, or indeed an invention?
Clause 5(4) of the Bill mandates that every police officer who receives or acquires knowledge of the warrant shall assist in the search for the missing child. Again, I suggest that the proposed legislation is very heavy-handed. Police forces have many responsibilities, both demanding and conflicting. Those responsible for the day-to-day, indeed minute-to-minute, allocation of police time frequently have to make unhappy choices. Is this legislation intended to place in the hands of a distraught parent the incentive to bring criminal action against each and every policeman or policewoman not perceived to be searching diligently?
Surely those in charge of any local police force must have the authority to allocate resources as circumstances dictate. However well intentioned this subclause may be, in my view the wording would create many more problems than it solves.
A third area of concern is one that is not addressed in the Bill. What happens when the child voluntarily absents himself or herself because of child neglect or abuse? Under what circumstances is a missing child returned to his or her parent or guardian? Is it on all occasions, some occasions and, if so, which ones? If a neighbour's child comes to me with some reasonable story of abuse, am I required by law to return that child to the parent or guardian, or do I have the option of consulting appropriate authorities? According to Clause 7(3) which I described earlier, I am obliged to allow free access to the parent or guardian to my private property. Do I now have a fight with the parent over the child? Indeed, do I not have a responsbility to that child?
I have every sympathy with the Hon. Member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby) in his desire, indeed the desire of all Canadians, to see appropriate mechanisms put in place for the speedy and safe return of children who are legitimately identified as missing. No doubt, others will speak about the need for well thought out co-ordination of the various police forces and agencies who need to be involved. Co-operation is most certainly required in areas where legislation is inappropriate or ineffective. While Bill C-234 addresses some of the important issues, in my view it is defective, particularly in the areas I have illustrated. Time constraints do not allow me to explore some of the other areas.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I want to congratulate the Hon. Member on his very serious concern for the plight of missing children as expressed in Bill C-234. Missing children are a major concern in our society. As politicians, we cannot ignore the anxiety being experienced daily by so many Canadian families.
By introducing this Bill in the House, the Hon. Member has demonstrated his desire to help missing children and their families. His is a noble gesture. However, I believe that in its present form, the Bill does not answer its avowed purpose. One example, Mr. Speaker, is that it fails to consider the fact that many children run away from home because they have been victims of physical violence, mental crualty or sexual abuse. By doing everything we can to return these children to their parents we are not necessarily acting in their best interests.
Since under the Constitution, responsibility is shared in this area, the police come under both federal and provincial jurisdiction. Should a federal Minister give instructions to a police officer or a police force, he would clearly be ultra vires. Even if that were not the case, any legislation in this respect would require extensive consultation between the federal Government and the provinces. Indeed, some clauses such as Clause 7(3), could probably be challenged successfully under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Under the provisions of the clause, a warrant signed by a parent or parents would apparently be the equivalent of a search warrant issued by an officer of the court upon receiving a sworn statement. Once issued, the warrant would allow proceeding with search and seizure while ignoring the requirement for reasonable cause.
Furthermore, the Bill does not take into consideration recent measures to improve police procedures for intervening in this area, such as the creation of the RCMP's Central Registry on Missing Children and instructions from the RCMP to all detachments advising them to act immediately on all reported cases of missing children.
Currently, there is no evidence, Mr. Speaker, to support allegations that the police are not acting as they should in reported cases of missing children. In fact, police forces across Canada are providing the best of co-operation where the central registry is concerned. Research projects being conducted by the Department in four Canadian cities will also enable us to assess police action on reported cases of missing children. That study, once completed in March 1988, and the experience gained with the RCMP's central registry should provide the information needed to determine whether any additional legislative action is needed in that area.
This of course does not mean, Mr. Speaker, that I do not think something should be done for missing children. In that
Missing Children Search Act
area, this Conservative Government which I am proud to be part of has been and is still doing pioneering work. The Government already has acted on its commitment. In August 1986, for instance, the Solicitor General officially opened the central registry for missing children. By linking all police forces across Canada, that registry significantly contributes to effective steps being taken nationally to address the problem of missing children.
This however is merely a first step, and the Solicitor General has promised to co-operate with all the agencies involved in order to find the most effective, long-term solutions to the problem of missing children. Moreoever, thanks to the efforts made by a number of agencies and levels of Government, progress to some extent has been achieved. National and provincial groups such as Child Find Ontario and Enfants-Retour, to name but those two, have made us more aware of the problem and have provided valuable services to the victims and their families. The circumstances surrounding the disappearance of children vary. However, all those children have one thing in common-they are all in danger.
Children who have been abducted by strangers are most obviously in danger, and such incidents make front-page headlines. Fortunately, Mr. Speaker, they are rare. Still a child abducted by his mother or father after a divorce is also in danger, especially so if the parent involved decides to go in hiding to avoid being found.
As to run-away children, they have to survive in a cold and harsh world. They may have run away because they were sexually abused, illtreated or neglected, but once they hit the streets they may very well face worse conditions, easy prey as they are for pimps and drug pushers. They might even engage in criminal activities-breaking and entering or shoplifting, for instance-just to feed themselves, Mr. Speaker.
As a rule, police will be the first to be told a child is missing and it is their responsibility to decide whether a search ought to be organized and to find ways to warn other local, regional, national and even international police forces so they too will be on the lookout.
But, Mr. Speaker, what coordinated measures can we take? How do we go about coordinating searches to find thousands of missing kids? The establishment of the registry is a first constructive step, but obviously we still have a lot to learn. We are still not fully aware of the extent and nature of the problem, let alone the best ways to solve it. Greater police efficiency is only one part of the solution, Mr. Speaker. We need more communication and co-operation at all levels. The search for a missing child has to involve social agencies, a large number of departments at all government levels, volunteer organizations, professional associations and the private sector.
In April last, for the first time in Canada, representatives of all the groups concerned with the problem of missing children met in Toronto at a national seminar on missing children organized by the Department of the Solicitor General. The

November 25, 1986
Adjournment Debate
object was to better identify the problem and to open discussions on how to co-operate in finding solutions.
The Solicitor General agreed to provide further opportunities for pooling information, discussing experiences and establishing national strategies for all parties involved in child welfare and concerned with crimes committed against children.
It is also important, Mr. Speaker, to foster parent awareness of the need to caution children against the dangers of the streets. To that end, parents of course must themselves be better aware of the dangers involved.
Mr. Speaker, in the few seconds I have remaining, I believe that by unanimous consent we should refer the matter to the Standing Committee on Justice and the Solicitor General.
